papers.title: Probing topological edge states in multilayer dielectric photonic nanostructures
papers.abs: Topological photonics has recently attracted a significant attention, leading to many theoretical studies and predictions. However, direct experimental demonstrations of topology-driven effects, particularly in nanostructures, are rarely proven. In this work, we experimentally investigate multilayer photonic nanostructures composed of alternating subwavelength dielectric layers, arranged according to the topological Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By engineering different edge truncations, we probe different supported topological phases. Our theoretical predictions and experimental measurements reveal strong field confinement at the surface exclusively in the configuration supporting topological edge states, providing their localized character and topological origin. First, we demonstrate enhanced absorption in an ultrathin absorbing overlayer deposited on the surface when the topological surface mode is present, highlighting the potential for surface-sensing applications. Second, we observe enhanced second-harmonic generation in reflection from the surface, demonstrating the potential of topological states for surface enhanced nonlinear optics enabled by the strong localization of the electromagnetic field at the interface.

papers.title: Plasmon modes in three-dimensional multifold semimetals. I. Triple-point semimetal, its quadratic cousin, and Hopf semimetal
papers.abs: We study collective charge excitations in pseudospin-1 triple-point semimetals within the random-phase approximation, considering both the linearised model with a flat-band and its quadratic-corrected counterpart. We analyse their density response, Drude weights, screening, plasmon dispersion and damping, particle-hole continua, and Friedel oscillations from the long-wavelength to the arbitrary-momentum regime. The quadratic correction renders the flat-band dispersive and endows it with a Fermi surface, thereby affecting the overall response. Comparisons with Weyl and Hopf semimetals reveal how bandstructure and quantum geometry jointly govern collective charge dynamics. While the Drude weights are determined by the Fermi surface and band-velocities, interband screening, plasmon dispersion, and Friedel oscillations reflect the quantum geometry of the eigenstates.

papers.title: Orbital Angular Momentum Transfer and Beam-Quality Limits in Fork-Grating Electron Diffraction
papers.abs: We analyze fork-grating generation of electron vortex beams beyond the ideal single-mode approximation. The incident beam is described as a paraxial Gaussian ensemble with finite transverse momentum spread and a first electromagnetic Hartree phase accumulated before the grating. Within Fresnel propagation we derive an analytical expression for each diffraction order and determine the corresponding orbital-angular-momentum statistics. The mean OAM of a selected order remains fixed by the topological rule, $\langle L_z\rangle_m=mp\hbar$, while its variance is set by the residual transverse momentum spread of the beam prepared at the grating. For the Gaussian mixture, the transverse purity is $\mathcal P_{\perp,m}=[1+2(ΔL_{z,m}/\hbar)^2]^{-1}$. The observed annular profile is governed by a separate propagation-dependent blurring scale, so a beam can retain well-defined mean OAM while having low transverse purity or a partially filled vortex minimum. Within the radial phase-screen approximation, the Hartree self-field modifies the propagated profile while preserving the full-plane OAM moments and transverse purity.

papers.title: Optical parametric amplification of spatiotemporal optical vortices
papers.abs: Spatiotemporal optical vortices (STOVs) are structured light featuring a phase singularity in the spatiotemporal domain, exhibiting unique topology that couples spatial and temporal dimensions. To date, amplification of STOVs remains unexplored, and their wavelength tunability is limited by available light sources. In this work, we present the theoretical analysis and experimental demonstration of optical parametric amplification (OPA) of STOVs. The pulse energy of the STOV signal is enhanced by a factor of 60, while its spatiotemporal structure is robustly preserved. The generated idler inherits the phase-conjugated STOV topology with the opposite topological charge, governed by simultaneous conservation of energy, linear momentum, and spatiotemporal orbital angular momentum. The intrinsic wavelength-conversion capability of OPA further provides a route towards spectrally tunable STOV generation, spanning from visible to near-infrared wavelength regimes. This work paves the way toward further development of multi-stage amplification architectures, facilitating applications of wavelength-tunable spatiotemporally structured light at ultrahigh intensities.

papers.title: Non-Hermitian Statistical Geometry
papers.abs: Particle exchange in two dimensions gives rise to quantum statistics beyond the boson-fermion dichotomy, with central roles in fractional quantum Hall physics, topological quantum computation, and strongly correlated quantum matter. In conventional topological phases, microscopic exchange geometry is compressed into rigid braid and fusion data. We develop a theory of non-Hermitian statistical geometry in which relaxing Hermiticity softens these exchange data into a larger complex space of spectral and relative-geometric degrees of freedom. For two adjacent braid generators, a single projective exchange spectrum is insufficient: their relative eigenline geometry supplies an additional gauge-invariant modulus. On the generic irreducible two-channel branch, braid consistency locks these coordinates through an exact spectrum-geometry relation. Using Riesz projectors and Kato transport, we realize this geometry in a five-arm Kitaev-Majorana network and test spectral and relative-geometric responses in an independent two-dimensional four-vortex Kitaev model. Finite-time dynamics tests the exchange operation, microscopic fusion sewing tests its composition across fusion descriptions, and matched-spectrum controls isolate the role of relative geometry. Nonzero projective Kato curvature shows that braid-consistent, fusion-coherent exchange can depend on the control path. Non-Hermiticity thus exposes exchange geometry, braid consistency re-locks it, fusion coherence further constrains it, and projective flatness determines when geometric exchange becomes intrinsically topological.

papers.title: Chirality Inversion and Giant Optical Activity in Scalable Self-Assembled Metamaterials
papers.abs: Chiral materials manipulate light in ways that hold promise for sensing, imaging, and photonics, but producing such materials with strong and reproducible optical activity at large scale remains challenging. Here, we develop a scalable strategy to assemble hierarchical helicoidal metamaterials from metallic nanoparticles and chitin nanocrystals, a biosourced polysaccharide. Spontaneous co-assembly produces ordered chiral structures with strong plasmonic optical activity, reaching a dissymmetry factor of 0.55. The unprecedented ability to vary the helicoidal pitch allows control of the optical response, enabling inversion of optical handedness without changing the handedness of the template, effectively decoupling geometrical chirality from optical chirality. Remarkably, the gold nanoparticles can also be recovered from dry films and redispersed as colloids, introducing an appealing circularity concept for sustainable chiral plasmonic materials.

papers.title: On-chip optical isolators
papers.abs: Optical isolation suppresses back-reflections that destabilize lasers, produce parasitic interference, and increase crosstalk in photonic systems. Although free-space and fibre-optic isolators are mature, no broadly adopted on-chip technology yet combines strong isolation, low insertion loss, broad bandwidth, compact footprint, and scalable fabrication. The difficulty is twofold: Lorentz reciprocity must be broken, and every relevant backward spatial, spectral, and polarization channel must be suppressed. This Review develops a common framework for assessing proposed solutions. We first distinguish pairwise nonreciprocity from intensity-asymmetric transmission and from true isolation using the constitutive relations and scattering matrix. We then compare three physical routes to an integrated nonreciprocal response: magneto-optical bias, externally driven space-time modulation, and nonlinear optical processes. Topological and non-Hermitian systems are treated as cross-cutting design frameworks that can route, protect, or enhance an underlying nonreciprocal response, but do not by themselves break reciprocity. Finally, we examine fundamental constraints and practical trade-offs among isolation, insertion loss, bandwidth, footprint, modal coverage, drive requirements, and fabrication compatibility. The resulting mechanism-based perspective connects reciprocity-breaking physics to the requirements of scalable photonic integrated circuits.

papers.title: Emergent Non-Biorthogonal Born Rule at Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions
papers.abs: Non-Hermitian dynamics possesses distinct left and right eigenstates, but their normalization freedom obscures a direct probabilistic interpretation. Starting from a globally Hermitian system governed by the standard Born rule, we generalize dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) from a reference state to a physical subspace. This generalization provides a clear probabilistic interpretation of left and right states: when each state is normalized to itself, their mutual overlap determines a directly accessible dynamical transition rate. We discuss the new phenomena governed by this emergent non-biorthogonal Born rule and further identify a class of exceptional-point DQPTs (EP-DQPTs), at which the eigenstates of the critical propagator coalesce. Our theory places the probabilistic interpretation of non-Hermitian quantum mechanics on the firm footing of Hermitian quantum mechanics.

papers.title: A Full-Spectrum Theory of Moiré Superlattices
papers.abs: Conventional theoretical descriptions of moiré superlattices, epitomized by the Bistritzer--MacDonald continuum model, are fundamentally constrained by low-energy Dirac cone approximations and first-shell interlayer coupling truncations. While successful for small-angle twisted bilayer graphene near charge neutrality, these frameworks fail to provide universal analytical solutions for strained lattices, high-energy band behaviors, or arbitrary commensurate geometries. Here, we establish a unified, approximation-free analytical formalism for generalized moiré systems based on three pillars: (i) a rigorous two-dimensional-to-one-dimensional supercell cyclic mapping, (ii) exact block-circulant diagonalization of intralayer Hamiltonians, and (iii) quasi-degenerate Löwdin perturbation theory centered on arbitrary energy degeneracy points across the full spectrum. Unlike traditional schemes anchored to the Dirac point, our approach enables systematic perturbative expansions around any band crossing, unifying the characterization of low-energy flat bands with high-energy degeneracies. We demonstrate that this framework perfectly recovers the Bistritzer--MacDonald model in the low-energy limit while extending its reach to heterostrained systems and high-energy regimes. By incorporating high-order interlayer coupling shells, we reveal an intrinsic scale self-similarity in moiré lattices and predict the emergence of higher-order magic angles and tunable flat bands driven by secondary degeneracies. papers.title: Inverse design of poles and zeros: tailoring phase control in metasurfaces
papers.abs: We develop a physically interpretable inverse-design framework for generalized Huygens metasurfaces, using prescribed scattering poles and zeros to engineer resonance interference and transmission-phase control. Compared with direct optimization of transmission or reflection coefficients, this approach offers a physically transparent route to rationally controlling resonance properties, including linewidth and group delay, while reducing computational work. The resulting designs demonstrate how near-unity transmission and $2π$ phase excursion can arise from resonance interference. These signatures of the Kerker effect extend beyond the conventional alignment of electric and magnetic dipole resonances to other mechanisms, including guided-mode resonances and quasi-bound states in the continuum. We further optimize the Kerker condition across a continuum of refractive-index states in a reconfigurable phase change material metasurface, enabling high-transmission $2π$ phase tuning. Our results establish a versatile and practical approach to metasurface phase control through the targeted design of scattering poles and zeros.

papers.title: Imaging the topological sign of a Dirac mass with spin-polarized tunneling
papers.abs: A Dirac mass is characterized not only by its magnitude but also by its sign, which influences the Berry curvature, Hall response, and the propagation direction of chiral boundary modes. However, local spectroscopy of magnetic topological surfaces has so far accessed only the gap magnitude $|M|$. Here we show how the topological sign of $M$ can be determined locally. We first establish the sign information that spin-resolved tunneling can access and the reference required to obtain an absolute Hall sign. Although spin--orbital entanglement generally obscures the relation between measured spin and Dirac pseudospin, crystalline rotation symmetry alleviates this ambiguity at the band edge. On a $C_3$ axis, an axial tip couples to a fully spin-polarized state whose tunneling asymmetry directly reveals the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature, independent of orbital composition. We further show that the zeroth Landau level provides an independent mass-sign measurement with an unpolarized tip, while opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes provide self-consistency checks. These results pave the way for imaging the locations where the topological character changes within a material, rather than merely identifying where a spectral gap appears.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Chiral Perovskites for Polarization-Sensitive Photodetection
Spatial Engineering of Topological Quantum Matter with Structured Light
papers.abs: Structured light provides a powerful means of controlling matter while itself exhibiting nontrivial spatial topology. Here, we show that these spatial structures can be harnessed to locally engineer the topological properties of matter. In a paradigmatic example of a topological insulator with Dirac surface states driven by an optical skyrmion beam, we show that structured light spatially tailors the effective Hamiltonian, yielding position-dependent topological gaps and Dirac velocities. The resulting gap modulation can create topological and trivial regions separated by optically defined interfaces, without introducing material boundaries or chemical modifications. We further show that the geometry of these interfaces can be controlled through the spatial structure of the light, in particular its orbital angular momentum. Our results establish structured light as a route to dynamically pattern topological phases and open a broader perspective on the interplay between topology in light and matter, including the possibility of transferring topological characteristics between the two.

papers.title: Chiral Vector Beams for Topological Enantio-Sensitive Imaging
papers.abs: Molecular chiral discrimination is vital across chemistry and life sciences, yet optical approaches remain highly inefficient for small organic molecules. Here we turn vector beams, whose polarization carries a topological charge, into an efficient probe of molecular handedness. We show that the combination of a tightly focused radially polarized beam at the fundamental frequency ω and an azimuthally polarized beam at 2ω creates chiral vector beams, a locally chiral field with structured handedness. Using state-of-the-art computational modeling in the chiral molecule carvone, we show that the nonlinear response (notably sum-frequency generation) of randomly oriented chiral molecules to this chiral vector beam captures the fields' local handedness and is highly enantio-sensitive. The two enantiomers emit light at frequency 3ω with topological ring structures of different divergence, and thus the molecular handedness can be read out directly from the ring radius. The signal inherits the Poincaré index of the driving field, opening up new ways to robust, ultrafast, and and all-optical chiral discrimination.

papers.title: Skyrmion gears: translation-to-rotation conversion of skyrmion clusters along periodic substrates
papers.abs: We investigate how the translational motion of a compact skyrmion cluster can be converted into collective rotation through interactions with a periodic obstacle substrate. Using an effective particle model, we consider a seven-skyrmion cluster driven along a one-dimensional array of repulsive obstacle sites. For suitable obstacle spacings and interaction strengths, repeated interactions with the substrate produce coherent clockwise or counterclockwise rotation, giving rise to gear-like cluster dynamics. We characterize these states using the translational velocity, Hall angle, angular velocity, structural deformation, and a dimensionless gear ratio that relates cluster rotation to motion over the substrate periodicity. Dynamical phase diagrams identify rotating, nonrotating, wall-guided, transverse, and deformed regimes. We further show that coherent rotation persists in the overdamped limit, demonstrating that the conversion mechanism does not require an intrinsic Magnus force and may therefore extend to other driven cluster systems, including colloidal assemblies. These results provide a simple route for controlling collective rotation through structured substrates.

papers.title: Nontrivial topological properties from the cooperation of static perturbations and Floquet fields in type-II semi-Dirac semimetals
papers.abs: In this work, we present a comprehensive theoretical study for the topological and anomalous transport properties of type-II SDSMs under three scenarios, i.e., static symmetry-breaking perturbations, periodic Floquet driving by two-frequency orthogonally polarized light (TFOPL), and their cooperative effects in the hybrid scenario. We first show that a static mass $m_z$ opens a bulk gap and drives the system into a Chern insulator with Chern number $C^{\rm per}=\pm 2\,{\rm sgn}(m_z)$. In comparison, TFOPL alone only shifts the positions of Dirac points and cannot open a full gap. Nevertheless, it produces a Berry curvature odd in the $x$-direction, yielding a finite Berry curvature dipole (BCD) along $x$ proportional to the sine of the initial phase, while the $y$-component vanishes. The hybrid scenario, by contrast, exhibits a remarkably rich phenomenology. Specifically, its gap-closure criterion becomes cubic and thus admits up to three real roots when the effective parameter along the $x$-direction is negative, thereby producing multiple light-tunable gap-closing points and a series of topological phase transitions. In particular, the BCD exhibits a double-peak structure with strong enhancement near gap-closing manifolds and synchronized sign reversal of the full vector under external tuning. We further analyze the anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC), anomalous Nernst conductivity (ANC), and anomalous thermal Hall conductivity (ATHC). papers.title: Metasurface quantum graphs for polarization-independent certified randomness
papers.abs: Quantum random number generators are crucial for information security, yet existing implementations are hindered by bulky optics, device imperfections, and state alignment constraints. Here, using a compact metasurface platform, we achieve polarization-independent certified randomness by establishing a quantitative quantum graph framework. By mapping multi-channel nanophotonic responses onto graph vertices, we assign metasurface measurements an operational information-theoretic meaning, directly connecting weighted graph degrees to conditional min-entropy estimation. The resulting graph-certified measurements yield robust private randomness even under entanglement-based attacks without complex optics. Experimentally, we fabricate 4- and 6-channel dielectric metasurfaces to implement high-dimensional positive operator-valued measure graphs, successfully certifying randomness with heralded single photons and Poissonian light. By integrating complex quantum measurements into a single passive layer, our metasurface quantum graphs provide a scalable route for integrated quantum technologies.

Wilson-loop formulations of the spin polarization and the spin Chern number
papers.abs: In this paper, we derive the spin polarization and the spin Chern number in momentum and real spaces in terms of the Wilson loop in each spin sector. For these derivations, the spin matrix in the subspace of occupied or unoccupied states is generalized by the unitary rotation to prevent the spectral gap from closing. In the presence of a finite spin gap, the spin eigenvectors recompose the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian in two spin sectors. A dimensional reduction leads to the charge polarization in each spin sector in terms of the Wilson loop along the effective Brillouin zone (BZ) in one dimension (1D). A linear combination of the charge polarizations defines the spin polarization, which naturally quantifies the spin Chern number in momentum space. It is also shown that the spin Chern number is directly derived from the local Wilson loops on a discrete 2D BZ. The theoretical treatment is further generalized for real space in a supercell framework, which can deal with ordered and disordered systems in a unified manner. In this framework, the spin Chern number in real space is formulated in terms of the Wilson loop around the BZ boundary. These formulations are used to numerically evaluate topological phases in the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang model. Numerical results show an equivalence of the spin Chern number and the ${\mathbb{Z}_2}$ index.

papers.title: Chirally pinned flat bands, helical minibands, and bias-controlled topology of Jackiw-Rebbi states in a periodically modulated Dirac mass texture
papers.abs: Flat bands amplify interactions into correlated phases, and topological bound states are robust by principle; combining the two in a model that is both exactly analyzable and experimentally accessible is therefore especially desirable. Here we show that a square-lattice model with a slowly modulated Dirac mass texture, $m(x)=m+m_0\cos(2πx/L)$ with $L$ up to hundreds of sites, provides such a setting, without engineered geometries, lattice-scale textures, or long-range hoppings. Exact nesting reduces the problem, independently at each transverse momentum $k_y$, to a $1+1$ dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian with a position-dependent mass: every simple zero of $m(x)$ binds Jackiw-Rebbi zero modes, and the two walls of a period form an effective Su-Schrieffer-Heeger ring. The model interpolates between a chirally pinned flat band at large $L$, a helical miniband whose nodes are enforced by a boundary phase of the ring, and a bias-dimerized regime in which the sign of the bias sets a winding number. A central result is that the miniband bandwidth is not a single scale: a max-min measurement conflates three widths of different origin, the helical height $W_{\rm JR}$ exponential in the period, the zone-edge upturn $W_{\rm edge}\propto L^{-2/3}$ dominating at large $L$, and a bias bump exponential in $L$, so the flat band is robust against bias in the thermodynamic limit. papers.title: Supercell-enabled inverse design of boundary-state dispersion for group-velocity control in pseudomagnetic phononic crystals
papers.abs: Topological boundary states offer a platform for guided-wave propagation within bulk bandgaps. Their propagation characteristics depend not only on the spectral extent of the states but also on their dispersion within the operating bandwidth. A nearly linear dispersion provides more uniform group velocity across frequency, whereas a reduced slope enables slow-wave propagation. Despite advances in inverse design of prescribed dispersion relations and topological dispersion tuning, application-oriented characteristics of boundary-state dispersion have rarely been direct inverse-design objectives. Here, we develop a supercell-enabled, surrogate-assisted framework for the inverse design of boundary-state dispersion in a phononic crystal with pseudomagnetic fields. Area-preserving anisotropic deformation shifts the local Dirac points, and independent variation of 21 rows within the supercell provides distributed control over the boundary-state branch. A constraint-preserving surrogate reconstructs the dispersion from an initial frequency and positive frequency increments, with first- and second-difference losses introduced to capture local slope and curvature. Coupled with a genetic algorithm, the framework targets two prescribed-bandwidth design tasks: highly linear dispersion and slow-wave dispersion. For the former, finite-element verification yields relative group-velocity variations of 0.142% to 1.183% over prescribed bandwidths of 4% to 6%. For slow-wave designs, mean group velocities of 190 to 385 m/s are obtained over bandwidths of 0.2% to 0.8% while satisfying a 5% grou

papers.title: Multipolar Nanophotonics with Quantum Computers
papers.abs: Small particles respond to light through electric and magnetic patterns called multipoles. Their interference determines the direction of scattered light and affects the decay of nearby emitters. Larger nanoantenna arrays, metasurfaces, and other nanophotonic systems demand increasingly costly simulations to meet strict performance and reliability requirements. We show how to represent these responses with quantum bits (qubits) and use quantum circuits to calculate scattering and the Purcell effect, the change in an emitter's decay rate caused by its surroundings. The circuits can encode known multipoles or estimate unknown ones from Maxwell's equations at the particle surface. We test the method against classical theory using an ideal quantum simulator and real IBM and IonQ quantum computers. For a silicon nanoparticle of radius 78 nm illuminated at 679 nm, IonQ gives a forward directivity of 2.984, close to the ideal dipolar value 3, quantifying the concentration of scattered light in the forward direction. For an emitter 10 nm from a gold nanoparticle and emitting at 510 nm, IBM measurements yield a calculated total decay rate 20.48 times its vacuum value versus 20.47 from theory, with correction for errors in reading the qubit states. We also establish how the number of multipoles and the required accuracy set the demands on qubits and measurements. These results motivate quantum-assisted design studies of directional radiation and emitter decay in nanophotonic systems.

papers.title: Measuring higher-order bulk topology in a programmable quantum simulator
papers.abs: Topological insulators lie outside the standard Landau paradigm: Instead of being characterized by local order parameters and spontaneous symmetry breaking, their defining properties are encoded in the global structure of their quantum states and manifested as robust boundary states. Crystalline higher-order topological insulators can extend this principle by hosting localized corner modes in two and higher dimensions. Although these boundary modes can be detected spectroscopically through the local density of states, determining the underlying bulk topology, for example through nested Wilson loops, remains an outstanding experimental challenge. Here we use up to 728 qubits in a superconducting analogue-digital quantum simulator to realize and probe a hierarchy of one-, two-, and three-dimensional topological insulators governed by effective tight-binding Hamiltonians. By reconstructing complex propagators from real-space measurements, we obtain complementary boundary and bulk characterizations: local densities of states reveal localized boundary modes, whereas experimentally reconstructed band projectors yield bulk topological invariants, culminating in a three-dimensional octupole moment extracted through third nested Wilson loops. These results establish a route to realizing, characterizing, and manipulating topologically protected states in programmable three-dimensional quantum matter.

papers.title: Probing the wave-vector gap in nanoscale magnonics
papers.abs: Short-wavelength spin waves are central to miniaturizing magnonic devices and to studying exchange-dominated magnetization dynamics. Yet the wave-vector range between roughly 30 and 300 radians per micrometre has remained difficult to access experimentally, posing challenges for both excitation and detection. This Perspective reviews recent advances in emerging measurement techniques and discusses prospects for their future development. Optical and microwave techniques are restricted to the vicinity of the Brillouin-zone centre. Inelastic neutron, electron and resonant hard x-ray scattering cover the full Brillouin zone but lack the energy resolution needed for low-frequency magnons at intermediate wave vectors. This Perspective examines five emerging approaches that are beginning to close this gap: Mie-enhanced Brillouin light scattering, colour-centre magnetometry, magnon momentum microscopy, extreme-ultraviolet transient-grating spectroscopy, and time-resolved scanning transmission x-ray microscopy. For each, we discuss the physical principle, demonstrated capabilities, current limitations and prospects for development. Compared side by side, the techniques give complementary access to magnon frequencies, local stray fields, real-space dynamics and momentum-space distributions, and they differ in their sensitivity to coherent and incoherent excitations. We therefore discuss the main advantages and use cases of each technique and consider the practical requirements for addressing different scientific questions. We highlight opportunities for further development, including

papers.title: Unlocking the potential of polymer networks for high strength through topology
papers.abs: A covalent polymer network is orders of magnitude weaker than individual covalent bonds. This large gap reveals an unrealized potential. The weakness of a network comes not from individual covalent bonds, but from how they are connected. Here we unlock this potential by identifying a topological criterion, involving optimally sparse crosslinks, long chains, and dense entanglements. Optimizing each topological variable alone is insufficient for high strength, yet exceptional strength emerges when they are combined within a narrow regime. We describe the physics of this synergy, and use the criterion to strengthen networks widely used but known to be weak. For example, we prepare a polyacrylamide hydrogel of 90 wt% water, amplifying strength from a commonly reported value of ~0.1 MPa to ~6.5 MPa. The exceptional strength is achieved without sacrificing other properties, such as softness, toughness, and elasticity. The criterion establishes topology as a general design principle for strong polymer networks.

papers.title: Superlattice-Stabilized Fractional Chern Insulators in a "Berry Basin" Model
papers.abs: The discovery of integer and fractional Chern insulators in rhombohedral graphene, following their discovery in the isolated topological flat band in twisted MoTe$_2$, motivates a search for the conditions under which an electronic band can host a topological correlated state. In this Letter we introduce a ``Berry basin" model which captures the essential features of rhombohedral graphene: a dispersive band with a flat bottom, momentum-space winding of a ``layer" degree of freedom, and Coulomb interactions, while also including periodic potentials, enabling controlled studies of the interplay of quantum geometry, superlattice modulation, and electron-electron interactions in producing correlated topological states beyond the isolated topological band paradigm. While integer Chern insulators emerge at strong coupling without a superlattice potential, stabilizing the fractional state requires nonzero potential for all interaction strengths we access. We provide insight into the greater robustness of integer and fractional Chern insulators in rhombohedral graphene when electrons are polarized away from the moiré interface. Our results establish a new class of systems that host robust fractional Chern insulators and provide a controlled numerical platform to test competing theories of interacting topological phases.

papers.title: Observation of quadrature-dependent unidirectional flow of light
papers.abs: Unidirectional transport of light is a central capability in photonics, enabling critical functionalities such as isolation and routing. Ordinarily, this directionality depends on the mode of light, but not its phase. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate phase-dependent unidirectional transport of light for the first time. Specifically, we realize a system where conjugate quadratures of an optical field decouple and propagate in opposite directions. Our all-optical approach uses multiple pump frequencies in a high-$Q$ nanophotonic micro-resonator to achieve Hamiltonian programming through Kerr nonlinearity. Even though we rely on optical nonlinearity, our approach is not limited to any minimal power requirement on the signal. We demonstrate the ultimate limit of this by measuring the effect of quadrature-dependent transport on vacuum fluctuations. Our approach unlocks a fundamental new capability for controlling light, and can enable previously inaccessible regimes of phase-sensitive directional amplification, sensing, and routing.

papers.title: Extreme Localization via a Singular Edge Mode in an Asymmetric Linkage System
papers.abs: Mechanical localized modes generally retain exponentially decaying tails, whereas confinement to a single structural unit is difficult to achieve without resonators, flat-band lattices or topological design. To address this need, an asymmetric linkage system is introduced in which geometry tunes a boundary mode from finite localization to its extreme limit. Each cell comprises two unequal rigid bars connected by a torsional spring and is described by one generalized coordinate. Linearization and coordinate transformation yield a tridiagonal model and closed-form expressions for the edge mode frequency and spatial decay ratio. The analysis identifies the configurations supporting a singular edge mode at which its decay ratio vanishes, leaving only the boundary cell active in the linear regime. Simulations show near-complete localization under finite-amplitude excitation, and experiments reproduce the configuration-dependent transition from bulk transmission to boundary confinement. These results establish a minimal and analytically tunable platform for mechanical localization

papers.title: Selective spatiotemporal mode-locking in multimode Mamyshev oscillators
papers.abs: Spatiotemporal mode-locking (STML) in multimode fibers introduces spatial degrees of freedom for ultrashort pulse generation, yet flexible manipulation of transverse mode compositions within multimode solitons remains challenging. Here, we propose a spectrum-to-mode mapping strategy in multimode Mamyshev oscillators (MOs) to selectively synchronize specific transverse modes through synergistic cross-phase modulation and offset spectral filtering. Meanwhile, four-wave mixing acts to stabilize intermodal phase relationships, facilitating selective STML characterized by diverse mode compositions with matched group velocities. Spatiotemporal solitons containing the pure LP01 mode, degenerate LP11 modes, or LP02+LP21 composite modes are selectively realized and mapped across the parameter space spanned by intracavity gain and filter detuning. Furthermore, intracavity collisions between coexisting mode groups with disparate group velocities are demonstrated to enable dynamic mode selection. Beyond the simulation of six modes in graded-index multimode fibers, selective STML is also demonstrated in MOs based on step-index multimode fibers and fibers supporting more transverse modes, confirming the generality of our approach. This strategy offers a versatile and robust pathway for transverse mode regulation and provides new insights into full dimensional structured light manipulation in multimode ultrafast fiber lasers.

Near-focus intensity evolution of spatiotemporal optical vortex pulses and consequences for their nonlinear upconversion
papers.abs: Spatiotemporal optical vortex (STOV) laser pulses are attracting attention for their puzzling transverse orbital angular momentum (OAM) and propagation properties, which could determine their future applications. While the characteristic reshaping of their space-time envelope upon diffraction from the focal plane to the far-field is now well-established, the evolution of their intensity as they propagate has not been studied quantitatively, despite growing interest for their use in nonlinear optics and strong-field physics. Here, we explore experimentally and analytically the focusing dynamics of STOVs produced by a pulse shaper, and evidence a substantial longitudinal shift between the coordinate at which a circularly-symmetric STOV forms and that at which the pulse reaches its peak intensity. To illustrate some practical consequences for applications, we experimentally demonstrate how the yield of second-harmonic generation can consequently be maximized several Rayleigh lengths beyond the plane where the circular STOV really occurs. These results signal careful characterization of spatiotemporal pulses as a requisite for nonlinear optical experiments, and pave the way for finer control of complex laser drivers for light-matter interactions.

papers.title: Maximal Axion Optical Chirality Enabled by Degenerate Quasibound States in the Continuum
papers.abs: Axion quasiparticles introduce magnetoelectric coupling in topological materials, yet their optical signatures are intrinsically weak, severely limiting experimental detection and practical exploitation. Here, we demonstrate maximal optical chirality of axion quasiparticles by coupling them with degenerate quasibound states in the continuum (qBICs). By integrating three-dimensional topological insulators (3DTIs) with achiral photonic crystal slabs (PCSs), we reveal that axion quasiparticles induce an effective Zeeman effect that lifts the degeneracy of achiral qBICs in PCSs, splitting them into two nondegenerate high-Q chiral qBICs with maximally opposite chirality. These result in a more than 10^3- and 200-fold increase in the polarization conversion efficiency and Faraday rotation angle, respectively, compared to the intrinsic chiroptical response of bare 3DTI films. Moreover, circular dichroism and nonreciprocal optical responses are revealed as new key signatures for probing axion quasiparticles in 3DTI-PCS coupled systems. Our results provide a definitive route for observing axion quasiparticles and topological physics, while establishing a promising platform for controlling optical polarization, spin, phase, and nonreciprocal responses.

Direct Observation of Chirality-Dependent Berry Curvature Dipole via Cross-Axial Nonlinear Hall Effect in Trigonal Te
papers.abs: Quantum geometric quantities, such as Berry curvature (BC) and quantum metric, are known to govern the physical and topological properties of materials, making access to these quantities critically important for the comprehensive understanding of the materials. Chiral crystals offer a natural platform in which structural handedness can control quantum geometry and nonlinear transport, but direct experimental access to the quantum geometric quantities has remained elusive. Here, we show that trigonal tellurium (Te) hosts an enantiomer-dependent Berry curvature dipole (BCD) that can be accessed through the measurement of cross-axial nonlinear Hall effect (NHE), unlike previously studied in-plane configurations where the BCD contribution vanishes. Angle-resolved measurements on left- and right-handed Te devices reveal a second-order transverse response whose sign reverses with crystal chirality. The extracted cross-axial nonlinear susceptibility, $χ_{yxz}$, exceeds the in-plane susceptibility, $χ_{xxx}$, by more than two-folds, indicating a strong BCD-driven contribution. First-principles calculations attribute this behavior to a topologically nontrivial hedgehog-like BC texture near the H points and predict a BCD that reverses sign between opposite enantiomers, consistent with experiment. These results establish cross-axial nonlinear Hall transport as a symmetry-selective probe of chirality-controlled quantum geometry in tellurium and related chiral materials.

Emergence of quantum transport in SnTe films upon structural refinement
papers.abs: Topological crystalline insulators are distinguished from the conventional Z2 topological insulators by crystalline symmetry protection of the surface states. Quantitative characterization of these states requires magneto-transport measurements from which the phase coherence length and number of independent coherent channels can be extracted. Here we report such measurements on textured thin films of SnTe grown on Bi2Te3 buffered c-plane sapphire (Al2O3) by pulsed laser ablation. A post deposition annealing protocol was implemented to control the crystallographic texture, which reveals improved crystallinity and enhanced epitaxial alignment along the [111] direction in films annealed at elevated temperatures. The higher carrier density and lower resistivity seen in films annealed at 100 oC are suggestive of Sn vacancies which act as native acceptor defects, while films annealed at 200 oC approach the 1:1 stoichiometry. The magnetoresistance of all samples at T 20 K, the MR is small and positive, and deviates from conventional Kohler scaling. An approximate collapse of the MR curves between 50 and 250 K is obtained using an empirical temperature-dependent scaling factor, indicating that changes in the Hall-derived carrier density alone cannot account for the observed scaling behavior. These results demonstrate that post growth annealing strongly influences the interplay between stoichiometry, crystallinity, and coherent transport in SnTe thin films.

Statistical Optical Replication and Mixing of Spatial Information across Wavelengths
papers.abs: Accessing and combining the spatial information carried by light at different wavelengths is important for linking structured-light encoding with spectrally distinct detection channels. Here, we introduce a correlation-enabled linear-optical framework for cross-wavelength imaging, bidirectional replication, and spatial information mixing. Shared random holographic modulation establishes correlations between nondegenerate optical fields, allowing spatial information to be retrieved from joint intensity fluctuations. In the demonstrated replicator, a spatial pattern encoded at one wavelength is read out in the detection coordinates of another through intensity correlations. Selecting diffraction-order pairs produces correlation kernels containing either the product or the conjugate product of two input field envelopes. These operations reproduce the spatial algebra underlying sum- and difference-frequency generation, while the optical fields retain their original carrier frequencies. The theory accounts for wavelength-dependent propagation and coordinate scaling, linking the input structures to observable correlation patterns. Together, these results establish a common framework for cross-wavelength spatial information processing through engineered optical correlations and joint detection.

papers.title: Giant geometric nonlinear transport in inhomogeneously strained Bi$_2$Se$_3$ single crystalline slabs
papers.abs: Electrical transport in non-centrosymmetric materials exhibits a nonlinear conductivity tensor component that generates second-harmonic voltages in response to applied electric fields. Harnessing this effect is essential for developing zero-threshold electromagnetic energy harvesters and broadband frequency upconverters, both of which require maximizing the nonlinear responsivity. Here, we demonstrate that inhomogeneously strained macroscopic slabs of the topological insulator Bi$_2$Se$_3$ achieve a record-high nonlinear responsivity of $10^4\,μ$m/V: a six orders of magnitude boost compared to its thin-film counterparts. We attribute this giant enhancement to a classical geometric nonlinear transport effect, which is driven by complex strain gradients within the bulk material. Notably, a similar geometric mechanism known as geometric nonlinear Hall was previously observed only in microscale-patterned structures. Our findings establish macroscopic strain engineering as a powerful route to enhance nonlinear transport, with immediate relevance to a broad class of layered systems, including transition metal dichalcogenides and moiré heterostructures.

papers.abs: Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) is typically achieved by depositing the analyte on a metal or semiconductor substrate. We propose a bottom-up approach, enabling SERS by depositing a metal on the surface of the object being studied. A Mie-theory analysis of electric-field enhancement in dielectric core-shell particles is presented. A correlative approach combining SERS, atomic force microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy is employed to model the conditions required for sensitive SERS detection and spectral analysis of polystyrene microspheres (PMSs) as models of globular and vesicle-like objects. Based on these findings, we propose a SERS-active system that provides strong signal enhancement (up to four orders of magnitude for a single globular object) while maintaining spectral fidelity, where PMSs act both as model analytes and as integral components of a metal-dielectric resonator.

Theory of exciton-exciton interactions with nontrivial electronic bands
papers.abs: Excitons are bound electron-hole pairs in semiconductors whose interactions influence optical properties and determine their collective behavior and emergent correlated phases. Despite the theoretical and experimental significance of these phenomena, a microscopic theory of exciton-exciton interactions that takes into account the full composite nature of these quasiparticles in systems with an arbitrary single-particle Hamiltonian is lacking. Here, we present a general theory of exciton-exciton interactions that builds upon our previous publication [Physical Review B 113, 155440 (2026)], which applied only to conventional semiconductors with weak band hybridization. By contrast, the theory presented here is valid in virtually any crystalline semiconducting system and can be applied to the study of biexciton formation and correlated excitonic phases in systems where band topology, quantum geometry, and moiré effects play a significant role. In addition to the analytical theory, we also present results in simple systems with flat bands with a nontrivial quantum metric and show that the biexcitonic spectrum differs strongly from that in the case without quantum geometry. Our theory paves the way for accurate quantitative calculations of biexciton spectra and excitonic many-body phases in modern condensed-matter systems.

Evolution and breakdown of chiral anomaly in Weyl semiconductor tellurium
papers.abs: Chiral anomaly in topological materials manifests as negative longitudinal magnetoresistance, yet the tunability and evolution of this effect remain elusive. Here we show that doped tellurium serves as a versatile platform to realize a giant negative longitudinal magnetoresistance that is highly tunable via the Fermi level and magnetic field. By moving the Fermi level towards the Weyl point, we observe a pronounced enhancement of negative magnetoresistance, which arises from chiral anomaly and robustly persists up to ambient temperature. Beyond the quantum limit, the system exhibits positive linear magnetoconductance, serving as a compelling transport signature of the chiral anomaly in the lowest Landau level. Notably, in the extreme quantum limit at cryogenic temperatures, the magnetoresistance undergoes a dramatic reversal from negative to positive. This reversal points to a potential field-induced phase transition into a collective electronic state driven by enhanced electron-electron interactions. Our findings provide valuable insights into the unconventional chiral transport and emergent correlated quantum states under extreme magnetic fields.

papers.title: Silent breakdown of the perturbative polarization expansion in the terahertz regime
papers.abs: Nonlinear optics expands the polarization in powers of the drive and retains only the lowest-order terms. This truncation is safe at optical frequencies, where the convergence field lies far above the damage threshold. In the terahertz regime, phonon polaritons enhance the nonlinear susceptibilities by orders of magnitude, lowering the convergence field into the sub-damage range and opening a window in which the expansion fails while the crystal remains recoverable. We term this window silent breakdown. At resonance, the nearest singularities of the driven lattice mode are a complex-conjugate pair of branch points below the multistability threshold, so the response remains smooth and single-valued even though the $χ^{\left( n \right)}$ description fails. The convergence field scales as $Q^{-3/2}$, so sharpening a resonance enhances the nonlinearity but narrows the range over which the expansion applies. It follows from the mode shift $S$ alone, $E_{\mathrm{conv}}=E_{\mathrm{ref}}(3\sqrt{3}QS)^{-1/2}$, giving 2$\sim$9 MV/cm for $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{3}$. Since resonant enhancement is central to terahertz nonlinear optics, this boundary defines the field range over which susceptibility-based descriptions are quantitatively reliable.

papers.title: Vacuum-field-mediated Landau-level reconstruction in a cavity-coupled two-dimensional electron gas
papers.abs: We study a two-dimensional electron gas in the integer quantum Hall regime coupled to a single spatially modulated cavity mode in the static off-resonant limit. Retaining both paramagnetic and diamagnetic contributions on equal footing, we derive a gauge complete single-particle Hamiltonian in which virtual photon exchange generates a periodic kinetic renormalization and a diamagnetic scalar potential. Both terms transfer momentum by $2k_0$ and displace guiding centers by $ΔX=2k_0\ell_B^2$, forming a finite-$k_0$ momentum ladder. Diagonalizing the strip Hamiltonian, we find that the ladder reconstructs the Landau-level band structure and redistributes, rather than multiplies, the associated chiral edge states. Occupied-subspace Chern numbers remain $C_ν=ν$ for $ν=1,2,3$ throughout $0\leλ_{\mathrm{cav}}\le 0.5$, while the bulk gaps decrease without closing. Strip Kubo responses show cavity-induced displacements of the Hall-step energies; at finite width the plateau heights are noninteger and approach the integers as $L_x$ increases. The ladder is spectrally resolved at $k_0\ell_B=0.5$ and collapses at $k_0\ell_B=0.1$. These results isolate a spatially local, finite-$k_0$ momentum ladder as a clean-system mechanism by which a structured vacuum field reconstructs quantum Hall spectra and strip transport without changing the integer topology, complementary to cavity-mediated all-to-all hopping.

Topologically steerable ultra-flat electro-optic combs via non-Hermitian frequency lattices
papers.abs: Electro-optic (EO) frequency combs convert microwave signals to the optical domain with deterministic repetition rates, enabling applications in optical telecommunications, microwave photonics, and LiDAR. However, generating flat EO combs has remained a long-standing challenge due to exponential decay of the spectral envelope inherent to bidirectional frequency coupling within conventional schemes. Here we reveal the inherent correspondence between flat-comb generation and the topological energy bands of non-Hermitian nonreciprocal frequency lattices, and experimentally realize ultra-flat combs with topologically controlled spectral flow. We derive the exact analytical condition for flat-comb generation, and find that it maps precisely onto the complex energy band, thereby establishing a direct connection between comb-envelope engineering and non-Hermitian topology. Experimentally, we observe an ultra-flat comb whose frequency evolution direction is governed by the topological winding and remains robust against detuning and phase fluctuations. This scheme can be further extended to long-range coupling and multi-lattice architectures, underscoring its versatility for flat dual- and multi-comb generation. Our work establishes a topologically steerable approach for achieving ultra-flat EO combs, paving the way for chip-scale spectral engineering via non-Hermitian topology.

The quantum geometry of the chemical bond
papers.abs: Electronic properties of materials depend both on band energies and quantum geometry of electronic states. We relate bonding indices to the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), showing how chemical bonding dictates the momentum-space texture of bands, bridging chemical and physical descriptions of solids. We show the QGT decomposed into the three center bond index, weighted by their oriented area. Resolving these contributions by orbital pair reveals the donor--acceptor character that distinguish ionic, covalent, hypervalent, and metavalent bonding. We identify the bonding pattern for topology in materials: noncollinear three center bonds, which are the source of Berry curvature in solids. Bond fluctuation can be directly linked to electromagnetic response by resolving their energy spectrum, opening a quantitative route towards the design of physical properties of materials from bonding motifs.

papers.title: Theory of Disorder-Induced Multimode Coupling in a Fabry-Pérot Cavity
papers.abs: Strong light--matter interactions have attracted significant interest in physical chemistry due to the potential for modifying molecular processes by hybridizing with cavity photons and forming polaritonic states. However, for a disordered molecular ensemble within an optical cavity capable of supporting multiple photon modes, theoretical understanding of multimode polaritons remains incomplete, particularly regarding whether and how distinct photon modes are mutually coupled through molecules. In this work, we generalize the collective mode expansion formalism to incorporate multiple photonic modes and show that spatial and orientational disorder in the light--matter coupling strength (originating from dipole orientation fluctuations and photonic field inhomogeneity) can mediate cross-mode coupling. This disorder-induced coupling allows for energy transfer to otherwise unexcited photon modes through a mechanism termed disorder-induced multimode activation (DIMA). Using an effective one-dimensional Fabry--Pérot cavity as a test system, we demonstrate that the cross-mode energy transfer through DIMA can be controlled by changing the molecular layer thickness and the optical properties of the mirrors. Furthermore, we show that DIMA is robust against weak energetic disorder. This mechanistic understanding lays the foundation for a systematic control of multimode photon coupling using disorder-induced effects.

papers.title: Search for free non-Abelian anyons in paired composite-fermion states
papers.abs: The even-denominator fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, understood as topological superconductors of composite fermions, are predicted to support elementary quasiparticles (QPs) or quasiholes (QHs) obeying non-Abelian braid statistics. Using the microscopic framework of parton theory, we investigate many experimentally observed paired composite-fermion states and find that their elementary QPs and QHs in general bind to form Abelian molecules, thus obscuring non-Abelian braid statistics. An exception is the $ν=1/2$ state in wide quantum wells, where our calculations show free QPs or QHs; we thus identify this state as an especially promising candidate for realizing and studying non-Abelian braid statistics. We also indicate how the study of such bound states can help reveal the topological structure of the state.

Frustrated Topological Orbital Magnetism
papers.abs: By studying the interplay of geometric frustration with Aharonov-Bohm fluxes in three dimensions, we unveil a rich playground exhibiting topological semimetallic ground states with orbital magnetic dipole, quadrupole and ferrotoroidic orders, akin to spin patterns in classical spin ices - a class of phenomena which we dub frustrated topological orbital magnetism. We demonstrate that the ground-state toroidizations underpinned by non-Abelian topological nodal lines induce measurable current-induced Hall phenomena. We further find that distinct 2-in-2-out and 3-in-1-out frustrated orbital current patterns can be associated with topological Weyl node charges, and corresponding anisotropic linear and nonlinear Hall effects. We propose signatures for experimental validation of distinct frustrated topological orbital magnetic orders in candidate materials.

Observation of robust corner states in photonic crystals without global symmetries
papers.abs: Robust corner states have attracted considerable attention in recent years, particularly in photonic systems. They are typically realized in second-order topological insulators, including shrunken-expanded lattices and breathing Kagome lattices, where global symmetries are essential in their formation. This reliance on symmetry, however, can make these states highly sensitive to structural disorder. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a class of robust corner states in photonic crystals that require neither global symmetry nor nontrivial topology. By locally tailoring the corner geometry of an otherwise topologically trivial structure, we create strongly localized modes that remain stable under both position and radius disorder. These states are not accidental; rather they originate from a pair of Dirac points in the bulk band structure. Geometric tuning shifts the flatband edge states connecting the Dirac points into an otherwise trivial bandgap, thereby inducing strongly localized corner states. Our findings uncover a previously overlooked class of symmetry-independent, disorder-resilient corner states, extend robust localization beyond conventional topological protection, and provide a route toward light localization in all-dielectric photonic systems.

papers.title: Symmetry-Dependent Polarity Reversal of Bulk Spin-Orbit Torque in Single-Layer MnCoGa
papers.abs: Controlling the magnitude and polarity of spin-orbit torque (SOT) is essential for manipulating magnetization in spintronic devices. Here, we realize bulk spin-orbit torque (SOT) in a single-layer Mn1.6Co1.4Ga (MCG) Heusler alloy and achieve lattice strain-controlled reversal of SOT polarity. SOT-driven magnetization switching is achieved over a thickness range of 3-20 nm, with the switching polarity reversed between the strongly strained ultrathin regime and thicker films. First-principles calculations reveal a sizable intrinsic spin Hall conductivity (SHC) in MCG originating from its topological band structure, which is enhanced by the tetragonal distortion without changing sign. Together with the thickness-dependent structural evolution, we demonstrate that the reversal of SOT polarity does not originate from a sign change of the SHC, but rather from lattice distortion induced symmetry breaking that modifies the conversion of spin current into a net bulk SOT, thereby controlling its polarity. These results establish strain-controlled structural symmetry as an additional degree of freedom for tuning bulk SOT in magnetic single layers.

papers.abs: We report, to the best of our knowledge, the first controlled, like-for-like experimental mapping of how four practical design parameters--seed-cavity topology, seed power, amplifier pumping geometry, and seed-cavity free spectral range (FSR)--jointly shape the radio-frequency (RF)-resolved relative intensity noise (RIN) of high-power continuous-wave (CW) Yb-doped fiber lasers. We compare a standalone bidirectional fiber Bragg grating (FBG) oscillator, an FBG-seeded master-oscillator power amplifier (MOPA), and unidirectional ring-seeded MOPAs with FSRs of approximately 11.5 and 5 MHz, all near 1064 nm at a common 72 W output, with RIN measured from 10 kHz to 1 GHz. Across all settings, the low-frequency RIN is technical-noise limited and nearly architecture-independent, whereas RIN above 160 kHz is governed by the seed-cavity topology and its transfer through the amplifier. Forward pumping gives the best power-scaling/noise trade-off, while reducing the ring FSR from approximately 11.5 to 5 MHz preserves the high-frequency RIN advantage, confirming it is not a mode-spacing effect. papers.title: Predicting plasmonic pole representations of complex dielectric spectra using convolutional neural networks
papers.abs: Extracting spectral properties such as energy position, broadening, and spectral weight from dielectric spectra is critical for interpreting collective electronic excitations in many-body physics. Conventional approaches typically rely on nonlinear fitting procedures that can be computationally demanding and highly sensitive to initialization and fitting choices. In this work, we develop a convolutional neural-network framework for the direct inversion of dielectric spectra into their underlying plasmonic pole structures using a multipole-Padé representation. Rather than training on a constrained database of spectra associated with a specific set of materials, the network is trained entirely on synthetic spectra generated from the analytical multipole-Padé expression with randomized parameters. This enables the network to learn the general mapping between the spectra and their features in an unbiased way, without requiring large, material-specific datasets derived from real materials. We demonstrate that the synthetically trained network generalizes to complex first-principles and experimental dielectric spectra, extracting the underlying pole parameters with high accuracy in a single forward pass. This approach provides an efficient and robust alternative to conventional nonlinear fitting, enabling high-throughput, automated analysis of dielectric spectra across diverse materials and applications.

papers.title: Robust skyrmion nucleation and transport via composition gradient in rare earth-transition metal ferrimagnets
papers.abs: Magnetic skyrmions are typically nucleated via localized excitation methods, such as laser heating, spin-orbit torques, or engineered defects, and their controlled transport is often limited by the skyrmion Hall effect. Here, we demonstrate that spatial gradients in rare-earth--transition-metal alloys, achievable through patterned laser writing, enable both deterministic nucleation and controlled transport. The strategy leverages engineered compositional gradient to cross the magnetization compensation point, defining regions with opposite magnetization. An out-of-plane magnetic field selectively reverses the magnetization, generating a skyrmion. Crucially, the same compositional design enables a channel tuned to the spin angular momentum compensation point, where skyrmions are driven by spin-orbit torques at high velocity with vanishing skyrmion Hall effect. Local composition variations act as pinning sites, enabling threshold-controlled trapping and release.

papers.title: Learning qBIC Resonances across Metasurface Families in Dielectric Fourier Space
papers.abs: Bound states in the continuum (BIC) metasurfaces are typically described by geometry-specific parameters, hindering cross-geometry comparison, while ultranarrow qBIC features are easily diluted in full-spectrum learning. Here, 2015 samples from seven dielectric metasurface families are mapped to a shared reciprocal-lattice grid, where two frozen low-order Fourier channels capture resonance shifts with mean within-branch $R^2$ values of 0.871-0.999. Field-level analysis of two representative branches further confirms that these shifts are consistent with the Maxwell-Fourier perturbation picture. A five-channel K-space backbone models the broadband spectrum, while a local complex K-space expert parameterizes the qBIC resonance through a differentiable Fano layer. The expert reduces resonance-position mean absolute error (MAE) from 3.2 to 0.95 nm and the resonance-depth error by 14-fold on a geometry-blocked test set. The same coordinate supports spectrum-to-structure reconstruction.

papers.title: Simulations of Fluorescence and Energy Transfer in Periodic Systems: Pitfalls and Considerations for Bound States in the Continuum
papers.abs: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) combine high quality factors with strong electromagnetic-field localization and are therefore widely explored for enhancing light--matter interactions. However, large field amplitudes do not directly translate into useful fluorescence enhancement or energy transfer enhancement between two donor--acceptor fluorophores. Here, we investigate this question for a hybrid plasmonic--photonic resonant waveguide grating supporting a symmetry-protected BIC. We emphasize some of the pitfalls associated with the numerical simulations, especially the utilization of periodic boundary conditions for fluorescence. Strong BIC-related fields can enhance acceptor absorption while useful fluorescence enhancement remains moderate. Extensive simulations and the comparison of different figures of merit, indicate that, while a BIC can suppress radiative leakage, it can also redirect a large fraction of the energy into Ohmic losses. As a result, the useful fluorescence enhancement of donors remains moderate, whereas absorption by acceptors can be strongly enhanced in Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) experiments. It is essential to separate near-field FRET from long-range energy transfer and reabsorption mechanisms, both of which are mediated by the delocalized BIC mode. Finally, results obtained for finite gratings are compared with infinite periodic simulations and conceptual inconsistencies explained. This work provides a consistent framework for interpreting fluorescence, absorption, and energy transfer in BIC-based periodic nanophotonic systems.

papers.title: Engineering Photon Avalanche Thresholds in Single Nanocrystals with Plasmonic Nanostructures
papers.abs: Optical sub-diffraction imaging has become an essential tool in modern research. Recently, a new imaging strategy has been demonstrated that exploits the strongly nonlinear excitation-emission response of rare-earth-doped nanocrystals operating in the photon avalanche (PA) regime. This approach benefits from simple optical instrumentation, near-infrared excitation and emission, low cytotoxicity, and high photostability. However, its practical implementation is hindered by relatively high (10-100s of kW/cm2) excitation power densities required to initiate the PA process. We aim to mitigate this limitation through electromagnetic field enhancement provided by metallic nanostructures. The results of microscopic studies of individual photon-avalanching nanocrystals coupled to a silver island film demonstrate a greater than tenfold reduction in the excitation power density required to trigger the avalanche emission. These experimental results, corroborated by numerical modelling, which elucidates the role of plasmon-mediated electromagnetic field enhancement in modifying the photon avalanche dynamics, paves the way towards new generation of low excitation power probes for sub-diffraction imaging and sensing.

Enhancement of the Topological Hall Effect through Engineering the Skyrmion Size and Shape
papers.abs: The topological Hall effect of skyrmions is a promising electrical probe of magnetic textures, but its small magnitude limits applications. In this work, we theoretically investigate the topological Hall effect induced by sparsely distributed skyrmions in the weak-coupling limit, focusing on how the size and shape of the skyrmion affect the Hall effect. To this end, we used a formalism based on angular-momentum eigenstates, which enables systematic analysis within reasonable computation time. We found that, in clean materials where the electron mean-free path is comparable to or larger than the skyrmion size, the Hall effect depends considerably on the size and shape of the skyrmion. In particular, the Hall effect is largest when $k_Fλ\sim 1$, and its magnitude can be tuned by the domain-wall width of skyrmions. These findings provide a basis for investigating how the shape and size of skyrmions affect transport properties and demonstrate that the topological Hall effect is controllable by engineering these properties.

papers.title: Analog quantum simulation of $φ^4$ field theory with a superconducting transmission line
papers.abs: Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum fields remains a fundamental challenge. We propose a superconducting transmission line for analog quantum simulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional $φ^4$ field theory. The transmission line comprises fluxonium-like circuit elements whose continuous and unbounded phase variables encode a scalar field without Hilbert-space truncation. Their anharmonic potentials provide strong interactions. Tuning the circuit parameters provides access to two distinct regimes. In the first, the transmission line emulates $φ^4$ field theory with a single-well potential. We confirm this correspondence through lattice Monte Carlo calculations of the low-energy spectra of both the circuit and lattice $φ^4$ theory. This regime enables scattering experiments between counter-propagating particle wave packets. The second parameter set yields a double-well potential that emulates $φ^4$ theory in the symmetry-broken phase and hosts degenerate vacua. Interfaces between the two vacua form topological kinks, and the transmission line can simulate kink-antikink collisions. We present state preparation and measurement protocols for both collision experiments, enabling spatially resolved, real-time studies of particle and soliton scattering in an interacting quantum field theory.

papers.title: Topological Spatiotemporal Mode-Locked Lasers
papers.abs: Achieving robust high-dimensional solitons both in optics and Bose-Einstein condensates remains a great challenge, due to unpredictable high-order perturbations. Here we propose and demonstrate a novel topological spatiotemporal mode-locked fiber laser empowered by mode-division multiplexing, for precisely controlling of the spatiotemporal solitons. By introducing time delays between the individual transverse mode paths, a topological spatiotemporal lattice is formed in the multimode cavity, which in turn excites periodic spatiotemporal solitons. These solitons are stable against the perturbations, attributed to periodic potentials induced by the nonreciprocal dissipative coupling interactions. Moreover, under the thermodynamic limit, the solitons condense into nested-type spatiotemporal solitons, a phenomenon analogous to the Bose-Einstein condensate of matter waves. Our results indicate that topological spatiotemporal mode-locked lasers not only constitute a controllable source of robust spatiotemporal light bullets, but also provide a valuable platform for exploring nonlinear high-dimensional soliton dynamics and non-Hermitian topological physics.

papers.title: Structured leakage in OAM-encoded qubits revealed by distributed quantum feature extraction
papers.abs: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes have emerged as an important platform for high-dimensional quantum communication but remain vulnerable to environmental noise and channel imperfections. Here we introduce a logical-qubit representation of OAM propagation in which modes evolve as qubits through noisy quantum channels. In this representation, turbulence manifests as leakage from the logical OAM subspace into turbulence-induced leakage components, providing a unified description of degradation in both single-photon and coherent-beam regimes. We show that turbulence-induced leakage exhibits systematic dependence on turbulence strength and OAM order, revealing structured signatures of information redistribution beyond the logical subspace. Leveraging this insight, we develop a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme that encodes high-dimensional OAM states into quantum representations and employs quantum convolutional operations to extract turbulence-robust features. Simulations and experimental measurements demonstrate robust extraction of these features across a broad range of turbulence strengths, OAM orders, and propagation conditions. Our results establish a direct link between OAM-channel dynamics, structured leakage, and quantum learning, providing a physics-informed framework for characterizing turbulence-degraded high-dimensional optical states and extracting robust signatures of turbulence-induced information redistribution.

papers.title: Decoupling ultrastrong Rabi splitting from quantum vacuum dressing in a chiral cavity
papers.abs: Polariton formation and quantum vacuum dressing are usually regarded as intertwined consequences of ultrastrong light--matter coupling. Here we show that they can be selectively controlled through the relative direction of rotation of the cavity field and the matter excitation. We consider cyclotron resonance coupled to a chiral cavity supporting a single circularly polarized mode. We quantize the electromagnetic field within the cavity, derive from first principles the Hamiltonian, and investigate how mode hybridization and vacuum dressing are rendered as we tune the magnetic field. When the cavity field co-rotates with the cyclotron motion, energy is exchanged resonantly between light and matter, producing a large Rabi splitting and conventional polaritons, while the ground state remains the bare vacuum. Reversing the magnetic field makes the cyclotron motion counter-rotating with the cavity field. The same cavity mode then couples through anomalous processes that create and annihilate light and matter excitations in pairs: the conventional polaritonic anticrossing disappears, while the ground state acquires squeezing and virtual excitations. Our results show that spectral hybridization and quantum vacuum dressing are distinct manifestations of ultrastrong coupling, offering an additional degree of freedom for engineering cavity quantum materials.

papers.title: Optimal Diffractive Focusing of Vortex Beams
papers.abs: We formulate diffractive ring focusing of paraxial beams carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM) through a finite circular aperture as a variational optimization problem. For a fixed topological charge, we determine the real-valued radial pupil that maximizes the intensity at a prescribed ring radius and propagation distance under a normalization constraint on the input field. The resulting problem admits an exact analytical solution: the optimal pupil combines the familiar Fresnel phase structure with an OAM-dependent Bessel radial modulation, and the associated eigenvalue yields a rigorous upper bound on the achievable ring intensity. We further analyze the lens-assisted configuration and derive a simple bound that allows direct comparison between diffractive and refractive vortex focusing. The theory also provides a quantitative framework for evaluating the performance of practical mask designs, including binary Fresnel-Bessel zone plates and amplitude-weighted pupils. We have experimentally tested our predictions in the optical domain by implementing the corresponding vortex beam pupils and comparing their propagation and focusing performance with the optimal solution. Our results establish the vortex-beam analogue of optimal amplitude-only focusing and identify the fundamental limits governing diffractive concentration of structured waves

Spin Chain with Continuous Exponential Symmetry: Topological Phase and Beyond
papers.abs: We study symmetric gapped ground states of one-dimensional spin $S$ chains with a continuous exponential symmetry $U(1)\rtimes\mathbb Z_2$ with integer base $q$, where the U(1) charge has a modulated unit of charge $q^{L-j}$ decaying exponentially with site $j$. The simplest model is a quantum breakdown model that can be viewed as a $q$-deformation of the XXZ Haldane spin chain. We show that the topology of their symmetric ground states crucially depends on $S$ and $q$. For integer $S$, odd $q$ allows a nontrivial $\mathbb Z_2$ Haldane-type symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase with protected edge modes, while even $q$ allows no nontrivial SPT phase. For half-odd integer $S$, odd $q$ prohibits any unique symmetric gapped ground state due to a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis obstruction, whereas even $q$ enforces a novel symmetric gapped phase which we name as the ``half-SPT" phase. Unconventionally, the half-SPT phase only has a symmetry protected edge mode on one edge, and has half of the string orders of an SPT phase. Our results uncover a new type of symmetry-protected gapped phases beyond existing classification schemes.

papers.title: SC$^\sharp$: superconductivity intertwined with topological order
papers.abs: Superconductivity and intrinsic topological order can intertwine in ways that go beyond simple coexistence. Here we develop a classification framework for (2+1)D gapped superconductors with condensate charge $2ne$. By focusing on the topological properties of superconducting vortices, we precisely characterize this interplay. We obtain a classification with increasing levels of intertwinement, from the well known invertible superconductors without topological order, to untwisted and twisted SC$^\ast$, and finally to SC$^{\sharp}$. Our main finding is the family SC$^{\sharp}$, in which the elementary vortex carrying $h/(2ne)$ flux cannot be factorized into an invertible superconductor vortex dressed by bulk anyons, and every elementary vortex is necessarily non-Abelian. For such phases, we also obtain no-go results: the elementary vortex sector has quantum dimension at least $\sqrt{6}$ and cannot satisfy Fibonacci fusion rules. We develop a systematic algebraic framework to obtain all these superconducting phases through anyon condensation, allowing us to construct several infinite families of examples and make connections to anyon superconductivity. Finally, we introduce primitive SC$^\sharp$ phases for which factorization of every nontrivial vortex sector is obstructed, and argue that they cannot arise by disordering the relative phases of lower-charge superconducting condensates. Our classification scheme based on vortex properties allows us to uncover new distinctions between topologically ordered superconductors and constrain how they can be realized.
